title: Subdural Empyema, Epidural Abscess, and Suppurative Thrombophlebitis

questions.question: Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.

parts.text: Name four cranial nerves that may be involved, with an associated sign or symptom for each.

parts_raw.text: Cavernous sinus thrombosis - 4 cranial nerves involved and an associated sign/symptom with each nerve

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Cranial nerve III (oculomotor) - ophthalmoplegia with ptosis and a dilated/sluggishly reactive pupil. (2) Cranial nerve IV (trochlear) - impaired downward and inward gaze (superior oblique palsy) contributing to diplopia. (3) Cranial nerve V (trigeminal, ophthalmic V1 and maxillary V2 branches) - facial pain and sensory loss over the forehead/midface. (4) Cranial nerve VI (abducens) - lateral rectus weakness causing lateral gaze palsy; because CN VI runs within the lumen of the sinus it is often the earliest nerve affected. Associated features include proptosis, chemosis, and periorbital edema, with bilateral eye signs as infection spreads through the intercavernous sinuses.

questions.question: A patient has an upper respiratory infection/sinusitis. A few weeks later they develop headache and low-grade fever. [image-based question: forehead abscess and a subdural abscess]
questions.question_raw: Patient upper resp infection/sinus. A few weeks later, headache, low grade fever.

parts.text: Name the syndrome and complication shown on the image (forehead abscess with subdural abscess).
Name the organism or group of organisms that is the most likely pathogen.

parts_raw.text: What is the name of the syndrome and complication (as seen on the image provided - picture of forehead abscess and a subdural abscess - Pott's puffy tumor)
What is the organism or group of organisms that is the most likely pathogen

questions.model_answer: a) Pott's puffy tumor - frontal sinusitis complicated by frontal bone osteomyelitis with a subperiosteal (forehead) abscess; the intracranial complication shown is a subdural empyema. b) Aerobic streptococci, particularly the Streptococcus anginosus (Streptococcus milleri) group, which dominate the flora of chronic sinusitis-associated intracranial suppuration (streptococci in 25%-45% of subdural empyema cases). c) (1) Staphylococci including Staphylococcus aureus (10%-15%). (2) Anaerobic streptococci. (3) Other anaerobes (e.g., anaerobic gram-negative bacilli). (4) Aerobic gram-negative bacilli (3%-10%); infections are frequently polymicrobial. d) Surgical drainage plus empiric IV antimicrobials directed at staphylococci, streptococci, aerobic gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes: vancomycin plus metronidazole plus a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone or cefepime), adjusted by Gram stain and culture; parenteral therapy for 3-4 weeks after drainage (longer with osteomyelitis).
questions.beyond_mandell: The eponym 'Pott's puffy tumor' is not used in this Mandell chapter; the entity (frontal osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess and associated subdural empyema) is established ID/neurosurgical knowledge.

questions.question: A 5-year-old child has orbital cellulitis complicated by cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.question_raw:
Q32 (2017)
5 year old child has orbital cellulitis complicated by cavernous sinus thrombosis.

parts.text: List 3 findings that suggest orbital vs pre-orbital cellulitis?
Fill this table regarding which cranial nerves are affected by cavernous sinus thrombosis and 4 common symptoms and signs: CN III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), V (trigeminal), VI (abducens)

parts_raw.text: A) List 3 findings that suggest orbital vs pre-orbital cellulitis?
B) Fill this table regarding which cranial nerves are affected by cavernous sinus thrombosis and 4 common symptoms and signs: CN III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), V (trigeminal), VI (abducens)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Proptosis. (2) Ophthalmoplegia with pain on extraocular movement. (3) Decreased visual acuity or afferent pupillary defect. (Chemosis and marked lid swelling also favour orbital involvement.)
b) CN III (oculomotor): ptosis, dilated/nonreactive pupil, eye deviated down and out, impaired adduction/elevation. CN IV (trochlear): superior oblique palsy — impaired depression of the adducted eye, vertical diplopia, compensatory head tilt. CN V (trigeminal, V1 ± V2): decreased sensation over the forehead and sometimes cheek (seen in ~25% of cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis, not typical of plain orbital cellulitis). CN VI (abducens): lateral rectus palsy — failure of abduction, esotropia, horizontal diplopia. Bilateral cranial neuropathies are typical, and contralateral orbital signs usually appear within 24-48 hours.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Proptosis, Pain on extraocular movements, Ophthalmoplegia, Diplopia, Chemosis.

B) III (oculomotor): Downward (SO4), outward gaze (LR6), dilated pupil. IV (trochlear): Hypertropia, head tilt. V (trigeminal): Deviation of the jaw, paresthesias, pain, inability to chew or bite down. VI (abducens): esotropia.
